extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of natural history, anthropology, and social/political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess 'progress' by the increase of heterogeneity (differentiation) across domains — geological, biological, social, linguistic, and artistic — as argued in the essay. The page supplies observable signs and examples of this law of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous
rubrics_metrics.description: The general law: progress consists in a change from homogeneous structures to more heterogeneous ones across natural and human phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central thesis repeated throughout: examples range from geology and climate through organisms and races to language, art, and social institutions. The essay uses this as the lens for evaluating historical advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological heterogeneity as evidence of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: No considerable portion of the Earth's exposed surface is like any other portion in contour, geologic structure, or chemical composition; heterogeneity increased by tectonic/igneous actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited causes include actions of the Earth's molten nucleus, tilting of strata, faults, veins, dislocations, changes in ocean beds, and resulting climatic differentiations (regions of ice, seasonal variation, tropics). Used as an instance of increasing heterogeneity over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological heterogeneity over geologic time
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisms have developed from the simple into the complex; later geologic periods show more heterogeneous organisms and assemblages than earlier ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by vertebrate sequence (Fishes → Reptiles → Birds → Mammals) and by the greater variety of mammalian orders/genera in tertiary than in secondary formations. Caveats about fragmentary fossil record and negative evidence are acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-species (human) anatomical and neural differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilized humans show greater internal heterogeneity (limb proportions, cranial vs facial bone ratios, more complex nervous systems) than less civilized races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Europeans compared to Australians in limb proportions; increased cerebrum ratio and convolutions. Infant developmental parallels cited as evidence of continuing differentiation from homogeneous embryonic forms to heterogeneous adult forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase in heterogeneity of mankind as a whole (racial differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The species Mankind has become more heterogeneous by multiplication and differentiation of races and tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnological divisions and philological evidence showing divergent tribes from common stocks are offered; recent emergence of new varieties (e.g., Anglo-American) are cited as ongoing examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and governmental differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress is shown by the differentiation of social roles and institutions: from homogeneous tribal members performing all functions, to distinct governing classes, religious institutions, ceremonial usages, and complex political organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stages: incipient chieftainship, hereditary rulership, the union/divergence of civil and religious power, emergence of church/state separation, development of courts, ministries, municipal bodies, ecclesiastical grades, and sects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregation into classes and division of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass of community becomes segregated into distinct classes and orders of workers, leading to minute division of labour and specialized producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traces evolution from tribal sameness to castes/guilds to modern specialized industries and interdependent localities. Notes economic specialization across districts/nations (calico in one county, woollen in another) and the role of improved transit and trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation and multiplicity in language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language advances from simple exclamations/noun-verb systems to many parts of speech, distinctions of mood/tense/person/number/case, auxiliaries, and a large heterogeneous vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also includes divergence of words from common roots into families, formation of derivatives and compounds, multiplication of languages and dialects through diffusion and local differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution of written language and pictorial systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Written language and pictorial representation differentiate from architectural/religious roots into picture-writing, hieroglyphics, hieratic/epistolary scripts, phonetic signs, alphabets, and eventually printing — each more heterogeneous in purpose and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Egyptian mural painting → picture-writing → hieroglyphics → hieratic/epistolary; use of phonetic signs for proper names as germs of alphabetic systems; Mexican picture-writing parallels; eventual divergence into multiple scripts and printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of artistic media and subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting and Sculpture separate from Architecture and from one another, and diversify into many subjects (historical, landscape, marine, genre, still-life, etc.), showing increasing heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical development from temple/palace mural decoration to bas-relief, free-standing sculpture, colored statues, and finally secular diversification in recent centuries; Christian art's religious origins and later secular split are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased structural heterogeneity within individual works
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern individual works (pictures, statues, written compositions) are internally more heterogeneous in structure than ancient ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted in the arts (modern pictures/statues vs Egyptian frescoes) and implied across cultural products: more varied elements, functions, and internal differentiation characterize later works.
